title: Printers Cost Less Than Ink—How Do Makers Profit?｜So That's Why
description:
Buying a discounted home inkjet printer feels like a steal—until the ink runs out and a full set of original cartridges costs more than a brand-new printer!
For anyone who has considered tossing an empty printer for a new one, wondered why third-party ink triggers error screens, or compared cartridge, big-tank, and subscription models.
From two myths in 1904 safety-razor history and the 1985 disposable thermal printhead breakthrough to aftermarket lock-in, microchips, firmware checks, opposing U.S. and Japanese Supreme Court patent rulings, and supplies generating nearly two-thirds of printing revenue, here is how the business really works.

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.
Data as of 2026-11-18.

chapters.kid-cartridge-vs-printer-scale: New Printer Cheaper Than Ink—Is It Charity?
chapters.kid-gillette-textbook-guess: Razor Pioneer Didn't Sell Cheap—And Makers Want a Lock
chapters.early-1980s-plumbing-inkjet: Disposable Thermal Printheads Bind Micron Ink Formulas Into One Cartridge
chapters.remanufacturer-refill-wave: Washing Empty Inkjets Ruled 'New Make' & Chips on Discount Toner
chapters.sept-2016-firmware-strike: 220k Undisclosed Blocks vs. U.S. Patent Exhaustion
chapters.chief-callback-opening-printer: Supplies Drive Two-Thirds of Revenue: Check Timing First

g001.text: Chief! My printer's out of ink—why does a set of original cartridges cost more than a brand-new printer?

g002.text: Did you almost toss the old one and grab a bargain printer instead? Makers price new machines that low on purpose!

g003.text: Because the real battleground in this business isn't the day you buy the printer—it's every refill after.

g004.text: Early printers cost a fortune; once cheap machines spread, one U.S. giant alone topped $10B a year from ink and toner!

g005.text: To guard that cash cow, some makers quietly blocked rival cartridges via code, while others sued refillers up to Supreme Courts!

g006.text: Today let's see how 'cheap printers, profit on refills' was born—and how makers lock down supplies!

g007.text: I've heard of this! Isn't it the textbook razor-and-blades model—sell handles at a loss and profit on blades?

g008.text: Half-true! UChicago scholars showed safety razors weren't sold cheap at launch:

g009.text: For 17 years after its 1904 patent, the pioneer sold its razor set for $5—about a third of the average U.S. weekly wage;

g010.text: Patents locked blade fit, dealers couldn't discount a cent, and it profited on both handles and blades!

g011.text: Patents ended in 1921 and rival blades poured in—it sold a $5 new set and slashed old handles;

g012.text: Annual handle sales doubled past 4 million! Next year rivals cut prices, and the maker teamed up with gum—buy gum, get a razor!

g013.text: More users boosted profits, yet unpatented cheap handles still fed rival blade makers—so printer firms later locked supplies tight!

g014.text: To cut machine prices without letting buyers pour in rival ink, how do you bind liquid ink to a machine?

g015.text: Ink tubes and printheads! Early-1980s inkjets fixed the head inside the machine with thin tubes and valves;

g016.text: That plumbing was pricey and failure-prone, keeping inkjets out of the affordable home market.

g017.text: Problem is: how do you ditch the tubes? In 1985 an electronics firm unveiled the first disposable printhead, opening the budget inkjet market:

g018.text: Engineers built a low-cost mass-produced printhead firing ink via tiny heaters, merging it with the reservoir into one disposable cartridge;

g019.text: Head cost fell to 1%—cutting tubes lowered machine prices and locked ink in cartridges!

g020.text: Okay, bundling head and tank makes sense—but isn't ink basically colored water outsiders could mix?

g021.text: Plain dyed water won't work! Before one small cartridge runs dry, tiny heated nozzles must fire over 8.5 million micro-droplets;

g022.text: Nozzles are so tiny that dyed water dries and clogs on air contact—and the first compact machine couldn't even fit a nozzle cap!

g023.text: Humectants stopped drying yet smeared on plain paper within 10 minutes, needing special paper early on—wet in nozzles, dry fast on paper is tough!

g024.text: Tough formula! What if someone cracks it, washes empty OEM shells, and sells cheap refills?

g025.text: A wave of cartridge remanufacturers grabbed market share that way! Once sales took off, a Japanese printer maker sued over cartridge patents.

g032.text: Wait—customers paid to own those empty cartridges! Doesn't reselling refilled ones legally count as repairing used goods?

g033.text: In 2007 Japan's Supreme Court unanimously ruled against the refurbisher—in this case it wasn't repair, but infringing 'new manufacture'!

g034.text: Why wasn't it repair? The tank had no refill hole; its patent relied on pressing two fiber pads tight so the seam held ink and blocked air;

g035.text: Yet 7 to 10 days after running dry, leftover ink caked hard in that seam—blocking new ink and air control, so drilling alone leaked!

g036.text: Drilling the top and washing out dried ink rebuilt that anti-leak seal—remaking the lost patented structure and crossing past repair!

g026.text: Dry-powder laser toner cartridges didn't cake shut like that, making patent wins harder—so one U.S. giant sold toner two ways:

g027.text: Buy full-price and dispose of the spent shell freely; buy the ~20%-off return-discount cartridge and terms allow one use, returning the empty shell!

g028.text: Problem is: once a discount toner cartridge leaves the store, how can a silent plastic box make sure buyers use it only once?

g029.text: That giant put a microchip on every discount cartridge—the moment toner ran out, the chip blocked the cartridge from reuse!

g030.text: Yet refurbishers still bought empty cartridges in the U.S. and abroad, devised ways to counteract the chip, and resold them refilled;

g031.text: With its tech barrier bypassed, starting in 2010 that laser-printer maker sued refurbishers in U.S. court for patent infringement!

g037.text: If refilling draws suits, what if shoppers buy brand-new rival cartridges? How else do OEMs block?

g038.text: Makers also use firmware-chip checks! Starting September 2016 in Australia, many users saw third-party cartridges suddenly rejected!

g039.text: Working rival cartridges suddenly showed 'damaged cartridge' errors, so buyers blamed the ink!

g040.text: Stranger still, Australian regulators found a major printer firm had 'Dynamic Security' locks blocking rival cartridges on ~220k machines;

g041.text: Some had it from the factory, others via firmware updates—without clear notice at purchase or update!

g042.text: In May 2018 regulators announced the firm admitted non-disclosure likely misled buyers, adding labels and a removal update;

g043.text: It also undertook to pay AU$50 each to over 2,000 affected customers!

g044.text: Australia targeted undisclosed locks—what about that 2010 U.S. patent lawsuit over discount toner cartridges? How did it end?

g045.text: Big reversal in America! In 2017 the U.S. Supreme Court decided that toner case by majority opinion—the opposite way!

g046.text: Think of a used-car lot: once a carmaker sells a car, its patent is exhausted—it can't bar repair or resale;

g047.text: Whether sold lawfully in America or abroad, the instant a toner cartridge is sold, patent rights are exhausted!

g048.text: And there's more! The maker may at most sue original buyers under contract law—never downstream refillers for patent infringement;

g049.text: Both back exhaustion: the U.S. barred contract patent suits; Japan's case saw 'new make'!

g050.text: Still, many avoid third-party ink fearing the maker will void the whole printer warranty if it breaks!

g051.text: Under U.S. law, generally not allowed! The FTC's 2021 report notes federal warranty law bars tying coverage to branded supplies;

g052.text: It directly cites printer ink—an exemption requires proving OEM-only necessity plus public interest;

g053.text: In 46 years after the 1975 law, just three waivers were filed nationwide—all three denied!

g054.text: Warranties can't force OEM ink—is chip checking illegal? In Jan 2023 Italy acted on two giants:

g055.text: Using non-punitive 'moral suasion,' regulators didn't ban firmware-chip checks—but required clear non-OEM warnings at purchase and updates!

g060.text: A Dutch third-party seller sued too! Per the maker's report, a Dutch appeals court ruled it lawful in Nov 2024; rivals appealed again!

g056.text: If chip checks aren't banned outright, why do regulators push so hard for upfront disclosure?

g057.text: Shoppers have a checkout blind spot! An FTC report on a 1992 Supreme Court copier case noted:

g058.text: If buyers can't tally multi-year parts costs upfront and switching brands costs money, fierce new-machine competition won't cut aftermarket prices;

g059.text: Same for printers: showing non-OEM limits before buying and updating lets buyers tally full cost!

g061.text: Speaking of lifetime total cost, on major printer makers' real financial statements today, which side brings the money home?

g062.text: Remember that printer cheaper than ink? Look inside a listed U.S. printer giant's FY2025 report:

g063.text: Of ~$16.7B in printing revenue that year, ink and toner supplies hit ~$10.9B!

g064.text: Hardware was ~$5.8B, just 35%—nearly two-thirds came from repeat supplies!

g065.text: Even wilder, its PC unit had a 5.3% operating margin that year, while printing hit 18.7%!

g066.text: Wait—stores now sell big ink-tank printers you refill from bottles without tiny cartridges; don't makers earn less?

g067.text: Payment timing shifted! Analyzing its own business, that maker notes big-tank models carry higher initial margins on day one;

g068.text: Without repeat high-margin cartridges later, though, overall lifetime profit per big-tank printer may actually be lower!

g069.text: How do you lock in long-term cash flow? Makers push monthly subscriptions, trading upfront revenue for steady monthly income.

g070.text: Simply put, whatever the model, makers calculate lifetime revenue—the difference is when they collect from you!

g071.text: So that's why! No wonder bargain cartridge printers are priced so low—the maker shifted collection to future refills!

g072.text: Exactly! Disposable printheads lowered upfront machine barriers in 1985, sparking 40 years of tech and legal battles.

g073.text: Next time you see a bargain printer in a store, do you know what to check before buying?

g074.text: Don't just stare at the machine's sale tag—check whether supply rules are transparent and estimate multi-year refill costs first!

g075.text: Tell us in the comments: is your desk printer a cartridge model, a big-tank model, or a shelf by now?
